claims.claim: Memory is the ability to store and retrieve information over time. The APA Dictionary of Psychology defines memory as the ability to retain information or a representation of past experience across some interval of time, based on the processes of encoding, retention, and retrieval; OpenStax Psychology 2e defines it as the set of processes used to encode, store, and retrieve information over different periods of time.

Memory is best understood as a set of processes, not a single thing: in some ways it is like file drawers where mental information is stored, and it is also a series of processes that decide how information gets filed and how it gets found again.

Psychologists distinguish three necessary stages in the learning-and-memory process: encoding (converting experience into a form the memory system can hold — the input of information), storage (retaining the encoded information over time), and retrieval (getting the information back out of storage when it is needed).

The three stages are interdependent: how information is encoded determines how it is stored and which cues will be effective at retrieval, and the act of retrieval itself changes the way information is subsequently remembered.

Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin (1968) proposed the model of memory in which information passes through three distinct stages of storage in order: sensory memory, short-term memory, and long-term memory.

Sensory memory is very brief storage of information from the senses in a relatively unprocessed form — up to a couple of seconds; visual sensory memory (iconic memory) holds an image for less than a second, while auditory sensory memory (echoic memory) retains sounds a little longer.

Short-term memory holds a limited amount of material for roughly 10 to 30 seconds; working memory is the related but distinct active system that holds information in a highly accessible state while a person works with it (e.g., mental arithmetic).

Long-term memory is a relatively permanent information storage system that enables a person to retain, retrieve, and use skills and knowledge hours, weeks, or even years after they were originally learned.

The three boxes are a model, not a literal map of the brain: there is no physical chamber corresponding to each store, and later models (notably Baddeley and Hitch's working-memory framework) refined the original scheme.

Long-term memory divides into explicit memory — memories that can be consciously recalled and reported, including facts (semantic memory) and personally experienced events (episodic memory) — and implicit memory — memories learned without awareness that are demonstrated in performance, such as procedural skills.

Identity and learning depend on memory: the episodes of one's life (episodic memory) and knowledge of the world (semantic memory) are stored and retrieved information, and the ability to retrieve information from long-term memory is vital to everyday functioning.

Memory is reconstructive, not a recording: remembering involves recreating an experience or event that has been only partially stored, using general knowledge and schemas, so memories can be edited and two honest people can remember the same event differently.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The terms 'short-term memory' and 'working memory' are sometimes used interchangeably.
positions: OpenStax Psychology 2e: short-term memory is more accurately described as a component of working memory — related, but not exactly the same.

APA Dictionary of Psychology: short-term memory is the reproduction, recognition, or recall of a limited amount of material after about 10 to 30 seconds; working memory refers to systems for the brief retention of information in a highly accessible state.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the two as closely related but distinct: short-term memory holds information briefly, working memory holds and actively manipulates it, following OpenStax's treatment and the APA's separate entries.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the three-store model describes real memory stages or is merely a useful abstraction.
positions: OpenStax Psychology 2e presents the Atkinson-Shiffrin model as the standard framework: information passes through sensory, short-term, and long-term memory in order.

Later work (Baddeley and Hitch, 1974) refined and partly replaced the original scheme with a multi-component working-memory model, and Noba notes that psychologists continue to debate the classification of memory types.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the three-box model as the standard introductory framework, attributes it to Atkinson and Shiffrin, mentions the working-memory refinement, and adds the honest note that it is a model rather than a literal place — consistent with both sources.

sourceRecords.title: Memory — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public JSON API (getdopdefinitions?q=memory). Entry defines memory as the ability to retain information or a representation of past experience, based on the mental processes of learning or encoding, retention across some interval of time, and retrieval or reactivation of the memory. Supports the lesson's working definition. Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: Encoding — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public JSON API. Entry defines encoding as the conversion of a sensory input into a form capable of being processed and deposited in memory, and as the first stage of memory processing, followed by retention and then retrieval. Supports the one-line encoding description. Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: Storage — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public JSON API. Entry defines storage as the state of an item that is retained in memory, after encoding and before retrieval. Supports the one-line storage description. Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: Retrieval — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public JSON API. Entry defines retrieval as the process of recovering or locating information stored in memory, and as the final stage of memory after encoding and retention. Supports the one-line retrieval description. Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: Sensory memory — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public JSON API. Entry defines sensory memory as brief storage of information from each of the senses in a relatively unprocessed form beyond the duration of a stimulus; iconic memory holds a visual image for less than a second, echoic memory retains sounds a little longer. Supports the sensory-memory description. The lesson's sparkler-trail example is original. Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: Short-term memory — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public JSON API. Entry defines short-term memory as the reproduction, recognition, or recall of a limited amount of material after a period of about 10 to 30 seconds, and links it to the dual-store and modal (multistore) models of memory. Supports the short-term memory description. Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: Long-term memory — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public JSON API. Entry defines long-term memory as a relatively permanent information storage system that enables one to retain, retrieve, and make use of skills and knowledge hours, weeks, or even years after they were originally learned, and notes its division into categories including declarative and procedural memory. Supports the long-term memory description. Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: Explicit memory — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public JSON API. Entry defines explicit memory as long-term memory that can be consciously recalled — general knowledge or information about personal experiences retrieved in response to a specific request — noting the term was proposed in 1985 by Peter Graf and Daniel L. Schacter and is used interchangeably with declarative memory. Supports the explicit memory description. Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: Implicit memory — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public JSON API. Entry defines implicit memory as memory for a previous event or experience that is produced indirectly, without an explicit request to recall and without awareness that memory is involved. Supports the implicit memory description. The lesson's bicycle example is original. Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: Reconstructive memory — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public JSON API. Entry defines reconstructive memory as the process of remembering conceived as involving the recreation of an experience or event that has been only partially stored, using general knowledge and schemas for what typically happens. Supports the honest note that memory is reconstructive, not a recording. Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: Psychology 2e, 8.1 How Memory Functions — OpenStax
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A open textbook. Canonical openstax.org URL registered; openstax.org blocks direct fetch, so the section was read via Internet Archive Wayback Machine capture 20260427175909 of the canonical URL on 2026-08-22. Supports: memory as the set of processes used to encode, store, and retrieve information over different periods of time; encoding as input of information, storage as creation of a permanent record, retrieval as getting information back into awareness; the Atkinson-Shiffrin (1968) three-stage model (sensory, short-term, long-term memory); sensory memory as very brief storage up to a couple of seconds; short-term memory as temporary storage lasting 15-30 seconds with working memory as the related active system (Baddeley and Hitch, 1974); long-term memory as continuous storage of unlimited believed capacity; explicit memory (conscious recall; episodic and semantic) and implicit memory (demonstrated in performance; procedural memory, priming, emotional conditioning); and the statement that the ability to retrieve information from long-term memory is vital to everyday functioning. The book footer states the book may not be ingested into LLMs without OpenStax's permission, so REFERENCE_ONLY; lesson prose is original, facts synthesized, no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Noba Project — Memory (Encoding, Storage, Retrieval) (Kathleen B. McDermott and Henry L. Roediger III, Washington University in St. Louis)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: memory as a single term reflecting a number of different abilities (working memory, episodic memory, semantic memory); the framing that memory is in some ways like file drawers where mental information is stored and also a series of processes (how information gets filed and retrieved); the three stages of the learning/memory process — encoding (initial learning), storage (maintaining over time), retrieval (accessing when needed); the interdependence of the three stages; episodic memory as the episodes of one's life and semantic memory as a storehouse of knowledge about the world; and the point that failures at any stage can lead to forgetting or false memories. Facts synthesized; all lesson examples are original.
